Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 6: Chemical Reactivity.
Car exhausts release harmful gases like carbon monoxide.
Catalytic converters use rare, expensive metals to turn them into less harmful ones.
Why do some metals react so easily, while others hardly react at all?
Let's find out.
Strips of magnesium, copper and gold are each held in a hot flame.
Predict: which metal will react most strongly with the oxygen in the air,
and which will not react at all?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Each metal is held in the flame for the same time.
The magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame.
The copper turns black on the surface.
The gold does not change.
Explain what you saw.
Magnesium is very reactive: it burns, forming white magnesium oxide.
Copper is less reactive: only its surface reacts, forming black copper oxide.
Gold is unreactive and does not react with oxygen, even when heated.
Metal plus oxygen gives metal oxide.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Most metals react with oxygen to form a metal oxide:
metal plus oxygen gives metal oxide.
But how fast they react depends on their reactivity.
Potassium and sodium react so violently with oxygen that they're stored in oil,
to keep air away from them.
Calcium and magnesium are less reactive, but still react well.
Magnesium burns in oxygen with a dazzling white flame, forming magnesium oxide.
Iron and zinc react slowly with oxygen.
That's why rust forms over time.
Copper is even less reactive: it only reacts when heated,
slowly forming black copper oxide.
Silver and gold don't react with oxygen, even when heated.
They keep their shine for a very long time,
which makes them perfect for jewellery and coins.
Iron isn't found pure in nature.
It's in rocks called ores, like haematite, which contains iron oxide.
In a blast furnace, the ore reacts with carbon monoxide to produce iron,
but this releases a lot of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas.
Another method is electrolysis:
passing an electric current through molten iron oxide splits it into iron and oxygen.
It's more expensive and uses lots of electricity,
so it's only more sustainable when that electricity comes from renewable sources.
Very reactive metals like sodium and potassium can only be extracted by electrolysis.

How do metals react with oxygen?

captions: Many metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
Potassium reacts even more violently than sodium:
it whizzes around on the water's surface,
and the heat can make the hydrogen burn.
Calcium is less reactive.
It reacts steadily with water,
forming hydrogen bubbles and a milky white precipitate of calcium hydroxide.
Test the solutions with Universal Indicator, and you'll find they're alkaline.
Magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water.
Heated, it reacts with hot water or steam,
but forms magnesium oxide instead of the hydroxide, an unexpected result,
called an anomaly.
Zinc and iron only react with hot water, and copper,
silver and gold don't react with water at all.
A small piece of calcium is dropped into cold water,
and the hydrogen it gives off is collected and measured every minute.
The volume rises quickly at first,
then levels off at about 80 cubic centimetres when the calcium is used up.
When the same mass of magnesium ribbon is used instead,
only a few bubbles form: less than 1 cubic centimetre in five minutes.
Pause and decide: which metal is more reactive with water,
and what evidence from the data supports your answer?
chapters: How do metals react with water?
Data: hydrogen made by metals in cold water

captions: Metals react with dilute acids to make a metal salt and hydrogen gas.
The salt depends on the acid: hydrochloric acid makes chlorides,
sulfuric acid makes sulfates, and nitric acid makes nitrates.
Sodium and potassium react far too violently with acids to try in the lab!
Magnesium fizzes vigorously in dilute hydrochloric acid, making magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
Zinc reacts more slowly, and copper doesn't react at all.
Even fizzy drinks are acidic, so aluminium cans need a plastic lining inside.
Gold and silver don't react with dilute acids, water or oxygen.
A substance that doesn't react with other substances is called inert.
Sometimes reactions make a mixture of products, and only one is wanted.
The rest are impurities, which must be removed,
for example from medicines and food.
The same mass of four metal powders is added, in turn,
to the same volume of dilute hydrochloric acid.
The temperature rise is measured.
Magnesium makes the acid 18 degrees warmer, zinc 6,
iron 3 and copper does not change the temperature at all.
Pause and decide: why can the temperature rise be
used to put the metals in order of reactivity?
chapters: How do metals react with dilute acids?
Data: temperature rise when metals react with acid

captions: Do you see a pattern?
A metal that reacts strongly with oxygen also reacts strongly with water and dilute acids.
So we can list metals from most reactive to least reactive: potassium, sodium,
calcium, magnesium, zinc...
...then iron, copper, silver and gold.
This list is the reactivity series,
and it helps us predict how a metal will react.
We use it every day.
Steel is galvanised with a coating of zinc,
which forms a protective oxide layer that keeps air and water away from the iron.
Catalytic converters use platinum, palladium and rhodium as catalysts:
substances that speed up a reaction without being changed themselves.
They turn harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones,
but these metals are rare, costly and mined in only a few places.
A strip of zinc is put into blue copper sulfate solution.
A strip of copper is put into colourless zinc sulfate solution.
Predict: in which beaker will a reaction happen?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Both beakers are left for twenty minutes.
In the first beaker,
the blue colour fades and brown copper coats the zinc.
Nothing happens in the second beaker.
Explain what you saw.
Zinc is more reactive than copper,
so it pushes copper out of its compound:
zinc plus copper sulfate gives zinc sulfate plus copper.
This is a displacement reaction.
Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc.
Pause and explain it in your own words.

Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Write the word equation for magnesium burning in oxygen.
Pause the video now.
Answer: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
Question 2: Why are sodium and potassium stored in oil?
Pause the video now.
Answer: They react very quickly with oxygen in the air.
Question 3: What salt forms when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Zinc chloride (plus hydrogen gas).
Question 4: Which is more reactive: copper or magnesium?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Magnesium – it is higher in the reactivity series.
